story: Jupiter is the king of our solar system, but a persistent myth labels it a 'failed star.' Science shows that is an insult to the gas giant. While it is the largest planet, Jupiter is only about one-thousandth the mass of the Sun. To actually ignite and become a star through hydrogen fusion, it would need to gain roughly 80 times its current mass. If it reached 13 times its mass, it would become a 'brown dwarf'—a strange hybrid too big to be a planet but too small to be a star. These objects are often called 'failed stars' because they can fuse deuterium, a heavy form of hydrogen, but not the standard hydrogen found in stars. The most mind-bending part? Even if Jupiter grew 80 times heavier, it wouldn't get much bigger. Because of intense gravity, brown dwarfs are roughly the same physical size as Jupiter, just much denser.
angle: Even if Jupiter gained enough mass to become a 'failed star' (a brown dwarf), it would stay roughly the same physical size while becoming massively more dense.
disputed: The exact mass multiplier needed for hydrogen fusion is cited as 75 times by one source [S1] and 80 times by others [S2, S6]; the script should use 'roughly 80 times' to be safe.
